topic: The Windmill Problem: A Dance of Geometry and Combinatorics
target_audience: High school students interested in competition math (IMO level concepts) and curious problem solvers.

sections.title: Introduction: The Infinite Spinner
sections.content: Introduce the physical metaphor of the windmill. Imagine a set of 'stars' (points) on a map and a 'laser beam' (line) that rotates. Hook the audience with the central mystery: If this beam keeps spinning and switching its pivot point, will it hit every star eventually?
sections.example: A tiny robot named 'Dusty' stands on a point in a field of 5 scattered points. He holds a long pole and starts spinning clockwise. When the pole hits another point, Dusty jumps to that new point and keeps spinning.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Rules of the Game
sections.content: Define the mathematical constraints clearly to avoid edge cases. Explain 'General Position' (no three points are collinear) and the 'Pivot' mechanism. Use visuals to show a line rotating around a fixed center until it intersects exactly one other point.
sections.example: Visual: 3 points arranged in a triangle. Show the line rotating 60 degrees from point A to point B. If three points were in a straight line, the robot wouldn't know which one to jump to first!

sections.title: The Mechanism of the Pivot
sections.content: Demonstrate the transition. When the line hits a new point, the 'pivot' point changes. Emphasize that the rotation direction (clockwise) never changes. Animate the line 'sweeping' through the plane like a radar.
sections.example: Graphical Animation: A blue line pivots on Point P. As it rotates, it strikes Point Q. The center of rotation instantly shifts from P to Q, and the line continues its clockwise sweep from its new position.

sections.title: The Hidden Invariant: The 'Balanced' Line
sections.content: Introduce the core insight needed to solve the problem: The 'Side-Count'. If we choose a line that splits the points into two equal (or near-equal) sets, what happens to that count when the line pivots?
sections.example: Visual: Color points on the 'left' side of the line Blue and points on the 'right' side Red. When the line pivots on Point P to hit Point Q, Point P moves to the other side of the line, and Point Q moves to the pivot. The total number of points on each side stays exactly the same!

sections.title: The 180-Degree Flip
sections.content: Explain the global behavior. After the line has rotated 180 degrees, it returns to its original orientation but is 'flipped'. Every point that was on the left is now on the right, and vice versa. This transition proves that the line must have passed through every point to 'swap' their positions.
sections.example: Imagine 5 points. The line starts with 2 points on the left and 2 on the right. After a half-rotation (180°), the 2 points that were on the left MUST have been crossed to end up on the right. Since this applies to any point, the 'Windmill' must visit everyone.

sections.title: Conclusion and Application
sections.content: Summarize the beauty of the problem: how a simple local rule (rotating and hitting points) leads to a predictable global outcome. Mention that this was the 'hardest' problem of the 2011 International Mathematical Olympiad, yet its solution is purely visual logic.
sections.example: Show a fast-motion animation of a 10-point windmill completing a full 360-degree cycle, highlighting how each point takes its turn as the 'heart' (pivot) of the system.
